reference.source: British Society for Haematology guideline / Postgraduate Haematology
clinicalPearls: Encompasses anatomical asplenia (surgical or congenital) and functional hyposplenism, in which the spleen is present but underperforms
Sickle cell disease is the classic cause of autosplenectomy, while coeliac disease is the commonest non-haematological cause and merits a low threshold to test for
Other causes include inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disease such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis, infiltration, splenic irradiation, graft-versus-host disease and advancing age
The peripheral blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, acanthocytes, Pappenheimer bodies and often thrombocytosis; a pitted or pocked red cell count quantifies residual function
The cardinal danger is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcus), which can be fulminant with high mortality
There is also increased susceptibility to severe malaria, babesiosis and Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis following dog bites
Prevention rests on immunisation against encapsulated organisms and influenza, long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, and a patient-held alert card with standby emergency antibiotics
Any fever in an asplenic or hyposplenic patient is a medical emergency demanding immediate empirical antibiotics and urgent assessment
reference.pathophysiology: The spleen filters the blood and provides key immune functions: macrophages of the red pulp remove senescent and abnormal red cells and clear opsonised and poorly opsonised encapsulated bacteria, while the white pulp supports antibody production including protective IgM from marginal-zone B cells. When splenic tissue is absent or its microcirculation and macrophage function are impaired, these roles are lost. Incomplete clearance of red cell inclusions produces the characteristic blood-film changes, and defective clearance of encapsulated organisms together with reduced specific antibody leaves the patient vulnerable to rapidly progressive bacteraemia. In functional hyposplenism the mechanism varies with the cause, from microvascular occlusion and repeated infarction in sickle cell disease to reticuloendothelial blockade, congestion or infiltration in other disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies causing autosplenectomy
Coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease
Autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis
Prior splenic irradiation or splenic embolisation
Other primary immunodeficiencies causing recurrent encapsulated organism infection
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells and Pappenheimer bodies
Pitted (pocked) red cell count by interference-contrast microscopy or flow cytometry to quantify function
Abdominal ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging to assess splenic size or absence
Coeliac serology such as tissue transglutaminase antibodies
Autoimmune and, where indicated, immunoglobulin and vaccine-response studies
Full blood count to characterise associated cytopenias or thrombocytosis
redFlags: Fever, rigors or any flu-like illness that may herald overwhelming sepsis
Rapidly progressive shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Recent dog bite with malaise, raising the possibility of Capnocytophaga sepsis
Travel to a malarial area with febrile illness
reference.prognosis: With appropriate immunisation, antibiotic prophylaxis and patient education the risk of serious infection is substantially reduced, though it persists lifelong. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection carries a high mortality when treatment is delayed, so prompt recognition is decisive.
pitfalls: Failing to vaccinate and provide prophylaxis in functional hyposplenism, such as coeliac disease, because the spleen is anatomically present
Delaying empirical antibiotics in a febrile asplenic patient while awaiting investigations
Poor timing of vaccination around planned splenectomy, reducing the immune response
Neglecting to issue an alert card, standby antibiotics and clear patient education
Assuming a single course of vaccination confers durable lifelong protection without planned boosting
references: British Society for Haematology guideline on prevention and management of infection in patients with an absent or dysfunctional spleen
